title: Buxa and Jayanti Treks: Fort, Ridge, Cave and Lake
meta_description: Walks in Buxa Tiger Reserve: Santalabari to Buxa Fort, Lepchakha at dawn, the Jayanti riverbed to Mahakal cave and Pokhri lake, with guides, fees and rules.
summary: The best walking in the Dooars is in Buxa Tiger Reserve. A 5 km stone path climbs from Santalabari to Buxa Fort; Lepchakha's ridge is 1.5 hours higher; from Jayanti, a riverbed walk leads to the Mahakal cave and a steep path to Pokhri lake. Homestays cost ₹1,200–2,000 with meals and guides ₹500–1,000 a day.

sections.heading: Walking country in the Dooars
paras: Most of the Dooars is flat, and its parks are seen from jeeps and towers. Buxa is the exception. Here the plains meet the Sinchula hills on the Bhutan border, and old paths climb from the forest edge to villages, ridges and caves that cars cannot reach. Buxa Tiger Reserve, created in 1983, covers roughly 760 km² of sal forest, river beds and hill forest, and much of the walking happens inside it.

None of these walks is a high-altitude trek. The highest point most visitors reach, Lepchakha, is a ridge village a little above Buxa Fort's 867 m. What makes them worth doing is the forest itself, the history at the top, and the chance to sleep in villages where the Dukpa community, of Bhutanese origin, has lived for generations. They suit anyone of reasonable fitness, including families with children over about eight, if you go slowly and start early. Leave the big rucksack behind: you will carry little more than water, a rain layer and a torch.

sections.heading: The walks at a glance
paras: Distances in the hills here are given locally and vary, especially where paths cross riverbeds that shift after each monsoon. Treat these as approximate.

sections.heading: Santalabari to Buxa Fort
paras: Santalabari, about 15 km from Rajabhatkhawa and 30 km from Alipurduar, is the end of the road, with a forest check gate, a few tea shops and porters waiting for walkers. Pay the forest entry fee here or at Rajabhatkhawa, about ₹100–300 depending on the season's rules, and show your ID.

The path climbs steadily for 5 km through mixed forest, paved in long stretches with old stones and crossing small streams. It gains a few hundred metres, so the gradient is gentle by hill standards; most people take two to three hours with rests, and less coming down. Butterflies are everywhere from October to April, and hornbills and barbets call from the canopy.

At the top is Buxa village, spread along a ridge, and a short walk on are the fort's stone ruins and memorial. This was a Bhutanese fort on the Buxa Duar, taken by the British in 1865, then a detention camp for Bengal revolutionaries from 1930 to 1937 and a refuge for Tibetan monks from 1959. Plaques recall the prisoners and Tagore's poem of 1931 for them. Stay the night: the light at dusk and dawn is the best part, and the walk down is easy in the morning.

sections.heading: Lepchakha at dawn
paras: Lepchakha is a small Dukpa village higher on the same ridge, about an hour and a half above Buxa on a steeper path through forest and terraced fields. Its open slope faces south, and on a clear morning the view runs over Buxa's forest to the tea gardens and the braided rivers of the plains, sometimes under a sea of cloud.

Either leave Buxa before dawn with a torch and a guide, or stay a night in a Lepchakha homestay and wake up with the view. Carry a warm layer; the ridge is windy in winter. Haze builds by mid-morning from March onwards, so the first two hours of daylight are everything.

sections.heading: Jayanti: Mahakal cave and Pokhri lake
paras: Jayanti is a forest village on the bank of the Jayanti river, which spreads into a huge pale bed of stones below the Bhutan hills in the dry season. Two walks start here, and both need a local guide, both for the route and because rules on entry change.

The Mahakal walk heads upstream along the riverbed, crossing clear channels on stones, before leaving the river for a steep climb to a limestone cave. Inside, dripping water has formed stalactites and stalagmites revered as forms of Shiva. Distances given locally are about 5–6 km each way; allow a full day, start by 7 am and be back before dusk, when elephants cross the riverbed. At Maha Shivaratri, in February or March, the path is crowded with pilgrims. Wear shoes that can get wet.

The Pokhri walk climbs steeply through forest for an hour and a half to two hours to a small, dark lake ringed by trees. The local story holds that its fish and turtles are sacred, and nobody fishes here. It is a place of worship; keep your voice down and leave nothing behind. The path is slippery and leechy after rain, so go in the dry months.

sections.heading: Buxa to Jayanti through the forest
paras: Local guides describe a forest trail linking Buxa village with Jayanti, roughly 12–14 km, which makes a fine two-day loop: walk up to Buxa from Santalabari, sleep there, cross to Jayanti the next day and leave from Alipurduar. It passes through the core forest of the tiger reserve, crosses streams and descends to the Jayanti riverbed. It should be done only with an experienced local guide and with the forest department's current permission, since parts of the reserve open and close for visitors. Ask at the Rajabhatkhawa forest office or your Buxa homestay, and check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: Two plans that work
paras: Buxa and Jayanti are about 30 km apart by road, so it is easy to combine them, with Alipurduar or Rajabhatkhawa as the rail gateway.

Two nights: reach Santalabari by late morning from Alipurduar or Rajabhatkhawa, walk up to Buxa and sleep in a village homestay. Walk to Lepchakha for sunrise next morning, come back for breakfast and descend to Santalabari, then take a car to Jayanti, about an hour, for a sunset on the riverbed and a second night. Leave from Alipurduar on day three.

Four nights: add a full day for the Mahakal cave from Jayanti, a morning on the Pokhri path and a jeep safari in the reserve from Jayanti or Rajabhatkhawa, booked through the forest department. With a guide and permission, replace the drive between Buxa and Jayanti with the forest trail. Budget about ₹2,000–2,500 per person a day including homestays, guides and local cars.

sections.heading: Guides, fees, seasons and safety
paras: The walking season is November to March, when paths are dry and leeches absent. October and April are possible; from May the heat, rain and leeches make walking hard work, and Buxa's tourism zones close in the monsoon, roughly mid-June to mid-September. Parts of the reserve were affected by the October 2025 floods. Rules on routes, entry fees and guides change; check current status before you travel.
list: Guides and porters cost ₹500–1,000 a day; hire them at Santalabari, through your homestay or at Jayanti.
Homestays in Buxa, Lepchakha and Jayanti charge ₹1,200–2,000 per person with dinner and breakfast; carry cash, as there are no ATMs.
Carry water, a snack, a rain layer and a torch; mobile signal is patchy on all these paths.
Wear long socks after rain against leeches, and shoes with grip for the stone path.
Stay on marked paths, never approach elephants, and be off riverbeds before dusk.
Leave heavy bags in your car or a Rajabhatkhawa lodge and walk up with one daypack.

faqs.q: How long is the walk to Buxa Fort?
faqs.a: About 5 km from Santalabari, the road head 15 km from Rajabhatkhawa. Most people take two to three hours up on the old stone path through forest, and an hour and a half down. The climb is steady but not steep. Porters and guides wait at Santalabari for ₹500–800 a day.

faqs.q: Can we stay overnight at Buxa?
faqs.a: Yes. Dukpa families run simple homestays in Buxa village and higher up at Lepchakha, charging ₹1,200–2,000 per person with dinner and breakfast. Rooms are basic and some bathrooms are shared. Carry cash, a torch and warm clothes in winter, since there is no ATM and power can be unreliable.

faqs.q: Do we need a guide for Buxa and Jayanti treks?
faqs.a: For Santalabari to Buxa Fort the path is clear and a guide is optional. For Lepchakha we recommend one, and for the Mahakal cave, Pokhri lake and the Buxa–Jayanti forest trail a local guide is strongly advised or required. Guides cost ₹500–1,000 a day. Check current forest rules before you go.

faqs.q: How far is the Mahakal cave from Jayanti?
faqs.a: Distances given locally are about 5–6 km each way, along the Jayanti riverbed and then up a steep path to the cave. The riverbed shifts after each monsoon, so the route changes. Allow a full day, start early, carry water and wear shoes that can get wet. Go with a local guide.

faqs.q: When is the best season to trek in Buxa?
faqs.a: November to March, when paths are dry, skies are clear in the mornings and leeches are absent. October and April are possible but warmer. From May, heat, rain and leeches make walking unpleasant, and the reserve's tourism zones close from about mid-June to mid-September.

faqs.q: Is there a trek from Buxa to Jayanti?
faqs.a: Local guides describe a forest trail of roughly 12–14 km from Buxa village to Jayanti, a long day through the core of the tiger reserve. Do it only with an experienced guide and the forest department's current permission, which can change. Ask at Rajabhatkhawa and check current status before you travel.

Very few, and you will almost certainly not see one. After no direct record from 1998, a camera trap in December 2021 photographed an adult male tiger in the East Damanpur range. Elephants, gaur, deer and leopards are present. Walk with a guide and keep to paths.

faqs.q: Is the Buxa Fort walk suitable for children?
faqs.a: Yes, for children of about eight and older who walk regularly. The 5 km climb is steady with places to rest, and the fort and village are an adventure. Start in the morning, carry water and snacks, and hire a porter for bags. Avoid the walk after heavy rain, when stones are slippery.

faqs.q: What is the entry fee for Buxa Tiger Reserve?
faqs.a: Forest entry and vehicle fees are modest, about ₹100–300 per person depending on the season's rules, paid at Rajabhatkhawa or Santalabari, with extra fees for safaris and cameras. Foreign nationals pay more. Carry your ID, and check current status before you travel.
